items_missed: The customer's name was never verified and was probably wrong all call. She introduced herself as 'Hi this is Clari' and Joanna answered 'Alright, thanks Darryl I think we already have a profile for you' — pulling a name off the record rather than confirming the one the customer just said. She then alternated between 'Darryl,' 'Daryl,' and 'ma'am' for seven minutes. The email on file also did not match what the customer gave ('I think I have an iCloud is that just the same?'), which is a second signal that this record needed verifying rather than trusting. Joanna checked the email and never checked the name.
Never asked 'how are you today?' — no warm-up at any point.

Stairs and floors were never asked at either end. This is an apartment-to-apartment move, Joanna collected both unit numbers at the very end of the call ('my current department is 12101' and 'The new one is 116'), and never asked what floor either unit is on or whether there is an elevator. That single missing question is what makes the 2.5-hour estimate unsafe — see the estimate note below.
Additional stops never asked.
Elevator and HOA access never asked. Parking was covered well, the rest of the access picture was not.
'Pricing is super simple' opener never used — the section opened with 'now how we work is that we charge by the hour for all of our services.'

Meet Your Mover was named but stripped of its actual content: 'Also meet your mover feature. Rest assured Daryl we don't take daily can track the workers. Our guys are the most of that movers in the industry, and we'll send you their names ahead of time.' The names land; the photo does not, and neither does the timing — the customer never heard that the email arrives a few days before the move. The flag counts because the feature was named explicitly, but the reassurance it is supposed to deliver was half-built.

The no-hidden-fees pitch was partial. 'Again no hidden fees of any type credit card fees, taxes. All of that is already included' names two items and stops. No fuel surcharge, no transportation fee, no assembly fees — which matters here because the customer immediately got confused about exactly that and had to ask ('No, no, he will know if you will charge us or anything'), forcing Joanna to clarify that the $70 covers fuel.

No sense-check anywhere. The pricing, the three differentiators, the no-fees claim and the clock all ran as one continuous block of roughly two hundred words, and the customer's entire contribution across it was eight consecutive 'Mm-hmm's. Not one 'does that make sense?'

No typical time range was ever given for the home size. Joanna went straight from the item list to 'we should be able to complete it within the minimum of two and a half hours,' so the customer has no benchmark and cannot tell whether 2.5 hours is normal or optimistic.

Specialty and fragile items never asked. The probe covered chairs, coffee tables, small tables, nightstands, patio furniture and garage — all volume questions — and never asked about a piano, safe, antiques, artwork, marble or glass.
Stairs were never explained as an estimate variable, because they were never asked about. The customer is told a flat 2.5-hour number with no 'if you're on a third floor with no elevator this moves.'

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. The customer is packing her own boxes, expects only five to ten of them, and is moving a short list of furniture out of a room in a shared two-bedroom apartment. No prep-saves-money framing, no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload,' no close. On a job quoted at the bare minimum this matters less for the bill and more for the clock: the difference between the crew walking into a staged room and a half-packed one is the difference between hitting 2.5 hours and blowing through it.

The booking attempt was never initiated by Joanna. The customer closed herself — 'Can I have that scheduled on Tuesday?' — and only then did Joanna add urgency ('Of course, I actually have one truck left for that day'). Holding the last-truck line until after the customer asks wastes it.
No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email.

No 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'I'll send everything in the email so you can review the details that we have discussed' and 'just review the details if you have any further questions let us know' come closer than anyone else's in this batch — the review instruction is there — but the ask is framed around questions rather than corrections and never routes the customer back through the email. Given that both the customer's name and her email address were already wrong or ambiguous in the system, this is the call in the sample that most needed a real verification loop.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The close went from apartment numbers straight to the sign-off.
No hours and no direct number or callback path given.

No upper bound on the estimate was ever offered. The customer asked directly whether $545 was the total — 'so then as in, that's like, the total, like estimate total' — and got 'Yes, ma'am. As long as the guys would be able to finish everything within twenty and a half hours, that's already the charge and there are no other fees outside of that.' The conditional is buried inside a garbled clause and the customer walked away hearing a fixed price, not a floor.
No rapport or lightness at any point in the call — the register never varied from transactional.
top_strength: Joanna's pricing and differentiator block is the best in this week's sample by a wide margin — 17 out of 20, where the next-closest call is 12 — and it is the one place a rep delivered the branded material as it is actually written rather than paraphrasing it into nothing. She named all three differentiators in sequence, and No Worries came out almost verbatim from the scorecard: 'we even include our no worries damage coverage which would give you up to $2,000 coverage for any repair, replacement reimbursement that's for accidental damages.' Nobody else in the sample said the brand name, the dollar figure, and repair-replace-reimburse in the same sentence; most said the word 'insurance' inside a list and moved on. She followed it with Meet Your Mover and then the On-Time Guarantee — 'And lastly on time guarantee if we run late we provide discounts by the end of the day' — which is the only On-Time Guarantee delivery in this batch that was volunteered rather than dragged out. The inclusions list was complete and specific: 'that already includes the two men and the truck, all the wraps, protect your furniture. If you need help with the reassembly, taxes, insurance, credit card fees, all of that is in the price. The only thing outside of the hourly rate is a one time travel fee of $70.' She scoped the one exception cleanly and then defended it correctly when the customer pushed back, without hedging: 'The $70 fee is already the fuel fee.' The probe is also strong. She used the school-bus equivalent — the only rep this week to use any plain-language anchor — and used it at exactly the right moment, on a customer who would not have known what forty feet looks like: 'for parking and the distance from the door to the parking how far are we walking, like, can we park in front of your door already or one school bus is about thirty to forty feet, is it just within that distance?' She asked the stressor question in near-rubric language ('do you have any special instructions concerns or stressors about moving in general that you want me to take note of at this time?') and got a real answer about the bed frame, which she resolved immediately. And when the customer's home size turned out to be ambiguous — a two-bedroom where the roommate has already moved out — Joanna made the right methodological call out loud rather than forcing the record: 'For the meantime I'll just put it within the typical size of a two bedroom. But let me have your item so I will just base the estimate on your items.' Estimating off the actual inventory instead of the square footage is exactly right.
coaching_note: Estimate-accuracy flag, and this one runs the opposite direction from the usual pattern — it is an apartment underestimate, which is the half of the problem that gets less attention and costs more when it lands. Joanna quoted the bare 2.5-hour minimum, $545 all-in, for a bed frame requiring disassembly, a mattress, a dining table, a sofa, an accent chair and five to ten boxes, out of one apartment and into another — and she never asked what floor either unit is on or whether there is an elevator at either end. She collected both unit numbers at the very end of the call and asked nothing about them. If the origin is on a third floor with no elevator, or the destination is, 2.5 hours is not reachable and this customer has been told a number that will be wrong on move day. Worse, she was told it as a fixed price: when she asked 'that's like, the total, like estimate total,' the answer was 'Yes, ma'am,' with the conditional buried. Two fixes, in order. First, the floor-and-elevator question is non-negotiable on every apartment move — ask it before the estimate, not after. Second, never quote the minimum as a total without an upper bound: 'Based on your items I think we land right around the two-and-a-half-hour minimum, so about $545. If the stairs slow us down it could run to three, which would be closer to $640 — you only pay for what we use.' That is honest, it protects the relationship, and it is exactly the transparency that moves the 45-46% number in the direction Cameron is asking for. Second priority: Save Your Ass is a zero, and on a minimum-quoted job it is the difference between the estimate holding and the estimate breaking. This customer is packing herself and has five to ten boxes. 'One thing that makes a big difference — anything you can get staged and boxed before Tuesday keeps us at that minimum. The small loose stuff, anything off the walls, whatever's still in drawers. If you can take a carload over yourself, even better. Does that make sense?' Fifteen seconds, and it directly protects the number she just quoted. Third: the differentiator block is excellent content delivered as a monologue. Two hundred words, eight straight 'Mm-hmm's from the customer, and no sense-check. The best differentiator explanation in the batch may well have been heard as noise. Break it into two chunks with a 'does that make sense?' in the middle — Joanna already has the material, she just needs to let the customer into it. Finally, fix the name. The customer said 'this is Clari' and was called Darryl for seven minutes. The system record was already wrong on the email; it was probably wrong on the name too. One line closes it: 'Just to make sure I have you right — I've got Darryl on the profile, is that how you'd like me to address you?' The agenda opener is a genuine hit here and worth crediting — 'what I need to do is just ask you some questions about the move so we can give you a more personalized estimate, okay?' has both the roadmap and the confirmation tag, and the customer answered it. It is thin, covering only the probe step rather than the whole call, and adding the pricing preview and the ten-to-fifteen-minute timeframe would make it complete.
phone_presence_notes: Polite, correct and well-organized, with the name used three times and a genuinely accommodating response when the customer pushed back on the box range ('Okay, ma'am. No problem. Thank you') — but the register never varies from transactional: no warm-up, no humor, no acknowledgment that a roommate moving out mid-lease might be a complicated situation, heavy repeated 'Yes, ma'am,' and a two-hundred-word pricing monologue that reduced the customer to eight consecutive 'Mm-hmm's.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace deduction rests on transcript evidence that could be either delivery or transcription. The pricing block contains several passages that are unrecoverable as written — 'for every move you know, one bedroom apartment, word Davao we sent out two men,' 'Our guys are the most of that movers in the industry,' 'we only charge in fifteen minute inter rolls,' and critically 'As long as the guys would be able to finish everything within twenty and a half hours' where the number should be two and a half. Audio is needed to confirm whether the customer actually received a coherent explanation, and the customer's near-total monosyllabic participation makes it impossible to read her engagement from the transcript alone.
